caption: How do you do on this neuroscience test? Do you know that at any given time, your brain doesn’t allow you to see all of reality, but only a portion of it? Be careful of what you train your brain to see #learn #brain #neuroscience #Science #DidYouKnow
author: Dr. Bing, MD MPH
transcript: Look at this image closely. You have three seconds to identify at least four red objects. Ready? Did you find at least four red objects? Well, that's actually not the test because the real test is did you notice how many green objects there were? Most of you probably didn't. And this is a really good example of how your brain can filter reality because your brain is not designed to see everything. Your brain is designed to see what it thinks is most important in that moment. When I told you to look for red objects, your brain literally filtered out other colors so you could focus. So in a sense, you're not seeing all of reality. You're seeing a filtered version of reality based on what your brain thinks matters. In medicine, this is why we're very careful. If you walk into a patient encounter looking for one diagnosis, you will find it and you might miss something else. So we're trained to constantly ask ourselves, what am I not seeing? But this applies to all of our lives. If you train your brain to look for negative things, for example, you will see negative things everywhere. But if you train your brain to look for opportunities, good people, things to be grateful for, you will start seeing those everywhere too. So remember that your brain finds what it looks for. So be careful what you train it to see.
title: Your Brain Only Sees What It Looks For
one_liner: Your brain filters reality based on what it's trained to notice, missing everything else.
key_points: When focused on red objects, your brain literally suppresses awareness of green ones — a live demo of selective attention
The brain doesn't show you all of reality; it shows a filtered version based on perceived priorities
In medicine, fixating on one diagnosis causes doctors to miss others — a dangerous cognitive bias
Train your brain toward gratitude and opportunity, and you'll start seeing those things everywhere
